The '''Old Campus''' is the oldest area of the [[Yale University]] campus in [[New Haven, Connecticut]]. It is the principal residence of [[Yale College]] first years and also contains offices for the academic departments of Classics, English, History, Comparative Literature, and Philosophy. Fourteen buildings, including eight dormitories and two chapels, surround a {{convert|4|acre|ha|adj=on}} courtyard with a main entrance from the [[New Haven Green]] known as Phelps Gate.

The Old Campus comprised most of Yale College's grounds between its arrival in New Haven in 1718 and its 20th-century expansion. Yale's first building in New Haven, the College House, was erected in 1718 on the Old Campus' southeast corner, fulfilling the city founders' wish to have a college near New Haven's [[Congregational church]]. It was joined by [[Connecticut Hall]] in 1750, a student dormitory and Yale's only surviving building from the colonial era. A linear building plan established in 1792, known as Old Brick Row, was the first campus plan in the United States and became a template for many American college campuses built in the 19th century. After 1870, the original plan gave way to the current quadrangle of dormitories, academic buildings, and chapels.

In addition to Connecticut Hall, the current buildings of Old Campus include most of the first year dormitories of [[Yale College]], [[Street Hall]] of the [[Yale University Art Gallery]], and two buildings used for religious purpose: [[Battell Chapel]], third in a succession of college chapels, and [[Dwight Hall]], formerly the College Library. Although the current buildings have been renovated and their uses changed during the twentieth century, all were completed before 1928.

==History==
[[File:The First Yale College House Diedricksen.jpg|thumb|right|275px|Reconstructed view of the College House, which stood from 1718 to 1782]]

===First building: Yale College House===
When [[Yale College]] moved to New Haven in 1718, the town constructed its first building, the "College House," at the corner of College and Chapel Streets, where Bingham Hall now stands. The wood-framed structure contained all the functions of the college: student rooms, a library, and a combined chapel and dining hall.<ref name="NHHRI">{{cite report |title=Yale Central Complex, New Haven Historic Resources Inventory |author=New Haven Preservation Trust |year=1984 |publisher=City of New Haven |url=http://www.cityofnewhaven.com/CityPlan/pdfs/HistoricInventory/NH%20HRI%201%20Yale%20Central%20Complex.pdf |access-date=4 April 2014}}</ref> Falling into disrepair, this building was torn down in stages from 1775 to 1782.{{sfn|Tolles|2011|pp=27}}

===Old Brick Row construction===
[[File:A View of the Buildings of Yale College at New Haven 1807.jpg|275px|thumb|right| Old Brick Row in 1807, viewed from the [[New Haven Green]]. Left to right: South College, First Chapel, [[Connecticut Hall|South Middle College]], Connecticut Lyceum, and North Middle College.]]

Beginning in 1750 with the state-financed construction of [[Connecticut Hall]], a student dormitory, the buildings of Old Brick Row were built over the next one hundred years. A chapel, later known as the Atheneum, joined the dormitory in 1761. During a 1792 disagreement over whether the next building should follow a linear pattern, preferred by Yale President [[Ezra Stiles]], or right-angular pattern, preferred by the [[Yale Corporation]] and the town, Stiles commissioned [[James Hillhouse]] and [[John Trumbull]] to draft first college campus plan in the United States.{{sfn|Tolles|2011|pp=29}} Trumbull's drawings chose Stiles' linear pattern, interleaving narrow, steepled buildings between long student dormitories. By 1824, Old Brick Row included four student dormitories, then known as "colleges," and between them the Atheneum (First Chapel), Connecticut Lyceum, and Second Chapel.<ref name="kelly">{{cite book |last=Kelly |first=Brooks Mather |title=Yale: A History |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |year=1974}}</ref> Around the Brick Row at this time were a chemical laboratory, a mineralogical building (the Cabinet), and the Second President's House, replacing one north of Elm Street.

[[File:Yale University Old Campus 1877.jpg|thumb|275px|right|Yale College in 1879, with Old Brick Row buildings and first new dorms. Of the depicted buildings only the Art School, College Library (L.), Connecticut Hall (S.M.), Farnam (F.), Battell Chapel (B.C.) and Durfee (D.) now stand.]]
The college gradually purchased parcels of land until it controlled the whole block by 1857.{{sfn|Holden|1967|loc=Part II}} Properties owned by [[Amos Doolittle]] and [[Benjamin Franklin]] were consolidated and demolished, as were the town jail and poorhouse. On newly acquired land surrounding Old Brick Row, administrators built the Trumbull Gallery (1832), Divinity College (1835), the College Library (1849), and Alumni Hall (1850). Of the fourteen Yale buildings completed by 1850, only two, Connecticut Hall and the College Library (now Dwight Hall), would stand fifty years later, and both survive today.

===Quadrangle plan===
In 1870, Yale President [[Noah Porter]] announced the "gradual abandonment and removal of the present buildings of the Brick Row," beginning with the construction of Farnam Hall.{{sfn|Holden|1967|loc=Part II}}  From 1870 to 1928, the college undertook a wholesale reconfiguration of its campus, tearing down the Old Brick Row and its satellites and erecting a perimeter of [[Victorian Gothic]] student dormitories around a central enclosure.{{sfn|Holden|1967|loc=Part II}} Where before it had been most prestigious to live off campus, the new dormitories became fashionable as the preserve of seniors. When [[residential colleges of Yale University|Yale's residential colleges]] were opened in 1933, the Old Campus transitioned to a home for the common First Year, with upperclassmen living in the colleges.

{{wide image|YaleOldCampus2009.jpg|850px|align-cap=center|Panoramic view of McClellan Hall, Linsly-Chittenden Hall, Dwight Hall, the [[Memorial Quadrangle]] and [[Harkness Tower]], Lanman-Wright Hall, and Durfee Hall}}

==Yale Fence==
[[File:The Old Yale Fence c1880.jpg|thumb|250px|Seniors socializing on the fence around 1880]]
In 1833, a [[picket fence]] encircling the campus was replaced with a rail fence, causing a major shift in the social patterns of the Old Campus.<ref name="Schiff1998">{{cite magazine |last=Schiff |first=Judith |title=Tales of the True Fence |date=June 1998 |magazine=Yale Alumni Magazine |url=https://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/98_07/old_yale.html |access-date=25 June 2015}}</ref> The Yale Fence, a wood fence with square posts and round rails that ran three sides of Old Brick Row, was the college's primary gathering place thereafter.  Students would claim sections by class year, with seniors taking choice seats along Chapel Street.{{sfn|Holden|1967|loc=Part I}}  However, as the modern quadrangle took form, the fence was gradually uprooted. In 1888, the displacement of its last section for Osborn Hall caused 2,100 alumni to write in protest.{{sfn|Holden|1967|loc=Part I}}

The Yale Fence Club, an undergraduate fraternal organization, was named in its memory. The fence currently lining the Old Campus' interior courtyard is modeled after the old fence, and pieces of the original are held in [[Sterling Memorial Library]].<ref name="Schiff1998"/>

==Student life==
[[File:NathanHaleStatue.jpg|200px|thumb|right|Statue of [[Nathan Hale]] in front of Connecticut Hall]]
Old Campus houses first years from ten of [[Yale College]]'s fourteen residential colleges. These students are assigned a residential college before starting their studies at Yale, live in Old Campus dormitories during their first year, and move into their colleges at the beginning of sophomore year. Students assigned to [[Silliman College|Silliman]], [[Timothy Dwight College|Timothy Dwight]], [[Franklin College (Yale University)|Benjamin Franklin]], and [[Pauli Murray College|Pauli Murray]] do not live on Old Campus but rather in their colleges for all four years.

Since the 18th century, Yale's Commencement ceremony has been held on the grounds of the Old Campus. Every May, approximately 10,000 chairs are set up for the event and college's Class Day, held the day before and featuring a distinguished speaker.

During the late 19th century, the Old Campus hosted an annual Tap Night for the upperclassmen on the Old Campus, where juniors were inducted into secret societies. An echo of the event occurs with the annual fall ''a cappella'' rush, where singing groups race to first year dorms to choose new members. Old Campus hosts several curricular activities, including First Year Olympics, a competition among the residential colleges, and Spring Fling, an outdoor concert.

==Statues==
There are bronze statues on Old Campus of [[Nathan Hale]] (1913, [[Bela Pratt]]), [[Theodore Dwight Woolsey]] (1896, [[John Ferguson Weir]]), and [[Abraham Pierson]] (1874, [[Launt Thompson]]). There are also statues of lions at the entrance to Lanman-Wright Hall. Before it was moved to [[Science Hill]], a statue of [[Benjamin Silliman]] stood in front of Dwight Hall.

Copies of the Nathan Hale statue were cast for the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], the [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]] (''see [[Statue of Nathan Hale (New York City)]]''), the [[Tribune Tower]] in Chicago (''see [[Statue of Nathan Hale (Chicago)]]''), and [[Fort Nathan Hale]].

'''Science Hill''' is an area of the [[Yale University]] campus primarily devoted to [[physical science|physical]] and [[biological sciences]]. It is located in the [[Prospect Hill (New Haven)|Prospect Hill]] neighborhood of [[New Haven, Connecticut]].

Originally a 36-acre residential estate known as Sachem's Wood, it was purchased by Yale in 1910 as a land bank. To expand the former [[Sheffield Scientific School]], the hill was allocated to large science laboratories and the main buildings of the [[Yale School of Forestry & Environmental Studies]]. Several laboratory buildings were completed in the 1910s, but most of the campus was completed during the build-up of scientific research after World War II.

== Geography ==

The topography of present-day Science Hill was primarily formed during the [[Wisconsinan glaciation]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Alter |first=Lisa |title=Geology of Connecticut |publisher=Yale-New Haven Teacher's Institute |year=1995 |url=http://www.yale.edu/ynhti/curriculum/units/1995/5/95.05.01.x.html |accessdate=2 March 2014 |archive-date=6 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140306202136/http://www.yale.edu/ynhti/curriculum/units/1995/5/95.05.01.x.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Laurentide Ice Sheet]] flattened the soft [[sandstone]] of [[New Haven Harbor]] but had less effect on its surrounding, hard [[trap rock]] formations like [[East Rock]] and [[West Rock Ridge|West Rock]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Dana |first=James Dwight |title=On the geology of the New Haven region with special reference to the origin of some of its topographical features |publisher=Tuttle, Morehouse & Taylor |location=New Haven |year=1870 |url=https://archive.org/details/ongeologynewhav00danagoog |accessdate=22 February 2014}}</ref> Science Hill is a portion of a [[sandstone]] [[drumlin]] that was sheltered from glacial erosion by a [[traprock ridge]], Mill Rock, to its north.<ref>{{cite book |last=Zeilenga de Boer |first=Jelle |title=New Haven's Sentinels |publisher=Wesleyan University Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-0819573742 |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/books/9780819573759 |accessdate=22 February 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Dana |first=James Dwight |title=On the Four Rocks of the New Haven Region, East Rock, West Rock, Pine Rock, and Mill Rock, in Illustration of the Features of Non-volcanic Igneous Ejections: With a Guide to Walks and Drives about New Haven |publisher=Tuttle, Morehouse & Taylor |year=1891 |url=https://archive.org/details/onfourrocksofnew01dana |accessdate=22 February 2014 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/onfourrocksofnew01dana/page/49 49]–50}}</ref>
The south–north rise of Science Hill is approximately {{convert|80|ft|m}} at a 4.5% [[Grade (slope)|grade]], processing northward to a [[summit|peak elevation]] of {{convert|150|ft|m}} above [[Metres above sea level|sea level]] near the [[Yale Divinity School]].<ref name="Nitsch">{{cite web |title=Yale Science Hill Master Plan |publisher=Nitsch Engineering |url=http://www.nitscheng.com/?t=1&DO=67&DI=2961&CAT=2920&format=xml&stylesheet=NE_Projects_Popup&p=5418 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151114210041/http://www.nitscheng.com/?t=1&DO=67&DI=2961&CAT=2920&format=xml&stylesheet=NE_Projects_Popup&p=5418 |archivedate=2015-11-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite map |publisher=[[United States Geological Survey]] |title=New Haven Quadrangle—Connecticut—New Haven Co. |year=1972 |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/uconnlibrariesmagic/4731471022/ |scale=1:24,000 |series=7.5 Minute Series |type=Topographic map |isbn= |id=41072-C8-TF-024 |ref=USGStopo |accessdate=22 February 2014 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402173025/https://www.flickr.com/photos/uconnlibrariesmagic/4731471022/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== History ==

===Sachem's Wood estate (1784–1910)===
[[File:View of New Haven, Conn. 1879, Excerpt of Sachems Wood.tiff|thumb|right|1879 perspective map of Sachem's Wood]]
The Science Hill site is not known to be inhabited until 1784, when it was purchased by [[James Hillhouse]], New Haven's largest landowner.<ref name="NHHRI">{{cite web |last= |first= |title=New Haven Historic Resources Inventory |publisher=City of New Haven |url=http://www.cityofnewhaven.com/CityPlan/pdfs/HistoricInventory/NH%20HRI%201%20Prospect%20Hill.pdf |accessdate=15 February 2014 |archive-date=10 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140310054649/http://www.cityofnewhaven.com/CityPlan/pdfs/HistoricInventory/NH%20HRI%201%20Prospect%20Hill.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Hillhouse built a wide road, now [[Hillhouse Avenue]], to extend to the foot of the hill, but planned to use the ridge itself for his own residence, and called the tract "Temple Square."<ref name="NHHRI" /> Hillhouse bequeathed the land to his son, James Abraham Hillhouse, who built a family [[estate (land)|estate]] known as Sachem's Wood, a name derived from European-descended Hillhouse's supposedly [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] facial features.<ref name="books.google.com">{{cite journal |title=The Hillhouse Place: Records and Memories of the New Site for Yale's Coming Expansion |journal=Yale Alumni Magazine |volume=19 |number=1 |year=1909 |pages=636–637 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pyM6AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA636}}</ref> A secluded [[mansion]], designed by [[Ithiel Town]], was finished in 1828 at the present-day site of [[Kline Biology Tower]].<ref name="NHHRI" /> Later, the surrounding lots were developed into [[revivalism (architecture)|revivalist]] mansions, but the large Hillhouse tract remained an undivided estate.

Science education at [[Yale College]] came in 1802 with the appointment of [[Benjamin Silliman]] as professor of chemistry. Although Silliman was given a basement laboratory on [[Old Campus#History|Old Brick Row]], sciences were marginal within the university's curriculum.<ref name="Adkisson1">{{cite journal |last=Adkisson |first=Kevin |title=How Science Was Built: 1701-1900 |journal=Yale Scientific |date=2 October 2010 |url=http://www.yalescientific.org/2010/10/how-science-was-built-1701-1900/ |accessdate=25 February 2014 |archive-date=10 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140310081710/http://www.yalescientific.org/2010/10/how-science-was-built-1701-1900/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1847, the [[Sheffield Scientific School]] was founded as a separate school of Yale, and it began expanding its campus between the university's main campus and Sachem's Wood. Although a corporate entity of the university, the school was socially and administratively separate from the rest of Yale. [[Yale College]] students did not attend Sheffield classes, and Sheffield students lived in societies and dormitories separate from Yale College students.<ref>{{cite book |last=Barber |first=William J. |editor-last=Barber |editor-first=William J. |title=Economists and Higher Learning in the Nineteenth Century |publisher=Transaction Publishers |year=1993 |chapter=The Fortunes of Political Economy in an Environment of Academic Conservatism: Yale University |isbn= 9781412822169 |page=141}}</ref> Over time, the division caused Yale's science education and research efforts to suffer.<ref>{{cite book |last=Geiger |first=Robert L. |title=To Advance Knowledge: The Growth of American Research Universities, 1900-1940 |publisher=Transaction Publishers |year=2004 |isbn=9781412840088 |pages=204}}</ref>

===Purchase by Yale and early growth (1910–1945)===
[[File:Sachem's Wood cropped.jpg|thumb|right|The Hillhouse family mansion at the present-day site of [[Kline Biology Tower]]]]
By the turn of the 20th century, there were few large, undeveloped tracts of land near Yale's campus. The largest was Sachem's Wood, which a group of Yale alumni purchased from the Hillhouse family in 1905, hoping to give Yale room to expand.<ref name="Kelly" />{{rp|331}} Seeking to build new science facilities and bring the Sheffield Scientific School under greater university control and strengthen university science research, Yale raised funds from [[Margaret Olivia Slocum Sage|Olivia Sage]] to purchase the estate in 1910, renaming it Pierson-Sage Square.<ref name="NHHRI" /><ref name="Kelly" /><ref>{{cite news |title=$650,000 To Yale Mrs. Sage's Gift |newspaper=The New York Times |date=1 January 1910 |page=3 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1910/01/01/archives/650000-to-yale-mrs-sages-gift-as-a-descendant-of-abraham-pierson.html |access-date=2 March 2014 |archive-date=10 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140310053842/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F20A12FB3C5417738DDDA80894D9405B808DF1D3 |url-status=live }}</ref>  It was the largest single acquisition of land since Yale's founding. The university drew up two early site plans for the property: a [[Frederick Law Olmsted]] site plan in 1905, and a university-wide [[Comprehensive planning|master plan]] by [[John Russell Pope]] in 1919. Neither was fully enacted, but elements of both are evident throughout the present-day site.<ref name="Adkisson2">{{cite journal| last=Adkisson |first=Kevin |title=Science Goes Up Prospect Street |journal=Yale Scientific |date=1 December 2010 |url=https://www.yalescientific.org/2010/12/science-goes-up-prospect-street/ |accessdate=16 February 2014}}</ref><ref name="Mills Brown">{{cite book |last=Brown |first=Elizabeth Mills |author-link=Elizabeth Mills Brown |title=New Haven: A Guide to Architecture and Urban Design |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1976 |isbn= 9780300019933}}</ref>{{rp|144}}

[[File:Sloane Physics Laboratory from front or north side.jpg|thumb|right|Sloane Physics Laboratory, the first science building completed after Sachem's Wood was purchased by Yale]]
Shortly after the land acquisition, a gift was received from brothers [[Henry T. Sloane|Henry]] and [[William D. Sloane|William Sloane]] for a new physics laboratory.<ref name="Kelly" />{{rp|331}} Within the decade, Yale built chemistry, zoology, and botany laboratories, and new buildings for the [[Yale School of Forestry & Environmental Studies|Forestry School]], and [[Yale Peabody Museum|Peabody Museum]], all in the [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] style popular at Yale in the early 20th century.<ref name=Holden>{{cite book |last=Holden |first=Reuben A. |title=Yale: A Pictorial History |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1967}}</ref> The new facilities allowed Yale to demolish its older science buildings on its central campus, including the original [[Peabody Museum of Natural History|Peabody Museum]] and Sloane Physical Laboratory, making room for the [[residential colleges at Yale University|residential college system]].<ref name="Alden Branch">{{cite web|last=Alden Branch |first=Mark |title=Snapshots of a bygone Yale |date=18 October 2013 |publisher=Yale Alumni Magazine |url=http://www.yalealumnimagazine.com/blog_posts/1602 |accessdate=16 February 2014}}</ref> Meanwhile, the Sachem's Wood mansion, preserved for the Hillhouse family in the purchase agreement, was increasingly surrounded by large laboratory facilities. After the death of the last Hillhouse heir, Yale demolished the mansion in 1942.<ref name="NHHRI" />

===Expansion of science facilities (1945–present)===
After [[World War II]], residential overcrowding and an influx of married students prompted Yale to build temporary [[quonset hut]]s on undeveloped areas of Pierson-Sage Square.<ref name="Kelly">{{cite book |first=Brooks Mather |last=Kelly |title=Yale: A History |year=1999 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=9780300078435}}</ref>{{rp|406}} The advent of the "atomic age" prompted a second period of laboratory building.<ref>{{cite book |first=George W. |last=Pierson |title=Yale: A Short History |publisher=Yale University |year=1976 |url=http://www.library.yale.edu/mssa/YHO/Piersons/A_short_history.html |archive-date=2020-07-02 |access-date=2014-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702053420/http://www.library.yale.edu/mssa/YHO/Piersons/A_short_history.html |url-status=live }}</ref> University president [[A. Whitney Griswold]] relied on modernist architects for these facilities, breaking with pre-war gothic fervor.<ref name=Carley>{{cite web |last=Carley |first=Rachel D. |title=Tomorrow Is Here: New Haven and the Modern Movement |date=June 2008 |publisher=New Haven Preservation Trust |url=http://newhavenmodern.org/system/dragonfly/production/2013/10/09/14_26_41_524_NewHaven_TomorrowIsHere_Carley2008.pdf |accessdate=22 February 2014}}</ref>{{rp|53}} He asked [[Paul Schweikher]] for a Gibbs Laboratory design, [[Eero Saarinen]] for [[Ingalls Rink]], and [[Philip Johnson]] for the Kline Biology Tower, Chemistry Laboratory, and Geology Building. Like Olmsted and Rogers, Saarinen and Johnson were also asked to improve the site plan. Saarinen's vision contributed modestly to the configuration, while Johnson's buildings gave Science Hill a central courtyard.<ref name="Mills Brown" />{{rp|144}}<ref>{{cite book |last=Rey |first=Michael |editor1-last=Pelkonen |editor1-first=Eeva-Liisa |editor2-last=Albrecht |editor2-first=David |title=Eero Saarinen: Shaping the Future |year=2006 |publisher=Yale University Press |chapter=The David S. Ingalls Hockey Rink |isbn=9780972488129 |page=[https://archive.org/details/eerosaarinenshap0000saar/page/243 243] |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/eerosaarinenshap0000saar/page/243 }}</ref>

In 1966, the construction of Wright Nuclear Structure Laboratory (WNSL), named for [[Arthur Williams Wright|Arthur W. Wright]], allowed Yale to house the first emperor [[Van de Graaff generator|Van de Graaff]] [[particle accelerator]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bromley |first=D.A. |title=The Emperor Tandem at Yale |journal=Journal de Physique Colloques |year=1969 |volume=30 |number=C2 |pages=44–46 |doi=10.1051/jphyscol:1969206 |url=http://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/docs/00/21/36/70/PDF/ajp-jphyscol196930C206.pdf |archive-date=2011-05-09 |access-date=2018-11-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110509180747/http://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/docs/00/21/36/70/PDF/ajp-jphyscol196930C206.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Bromley |first=D. Allan |title=A Century of Physics |publisher=Springer |year=2002 |isbn=9780387952475 |page=[https://archive.org/details/centuryofphysics0000brom/page/10 10] |url=https://archive.org/details/centuryofphysics0000brom/page/10 }}</ref> Once the most powerful accelerator of its type, it was decommissioned in 2011 as other particle research facilities became more useful to the field.<ref>{{cite news |last=Gershon |first=Eric |title=Yale prepares for atom smasher's farewell, sets stage for new physics era |date=25 February 2014 |publisher=Yale News |url=http://news.yale.edu/2014/02/25/yale-prepares-atom-smasher-s-farewell-sets-stage-new-physics-era |accessdate=27 February 2014 |archive-date=2 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140302070542/http://news.yale.edu/2014/02/25/yale-prepares-atom-smasher-s-farewell-sets-stage-new-physics-era |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2013, [[Karsten Heeger]] initiated a transformation of the WNSL accelerator facility into a state-of-the-art facility, research program, and community that is equipped to develop, build and use research instrumentation for experiments across the globe that investigate the invisible universe.  The new Wright Lab opened officially in a public opening ceremony on May 16, 2017.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Misenti|first=Victoria|date=2018-02-14|title=History|url=https://wlab.yale.edu/about/history|access-date=2021-01-13|website=Wright Laboratory|language=en|archive-date=2021-07-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709185652/https://wlab.yale.edu/about/history|url-status=live}}</ref>

At the end of the 20th century, Yale President [[Rick Levin]] announced new investments in sciences and medicine.<ref name="Fellman 2000">{{cite news |last=Fellman |first=Bruce |title=Serious About The Sciences |date=May 2000 |magazine=Yale Alumni Magazine |url=http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/00_05/science.html |accessdate=2 March 2014 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402115309/http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/00_05/science.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Arenson">{{cite news |last=Arenson |first=Kate W. |title=At Yale, a $500 Million Plan Reflects a New Age of Science |newspaper=The New York Times |date=19 January 2000 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/01/19/nyregion/at-yale-a-500-million-plan-reflects-a-new-age-of-science.html |accessdate=23 February 2014 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402233652/http://www.nytimes.com/2000/01/19/nyregion/at-yale-a-500-million-plan-reflects-a-new-age-of-science.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In the years following, the university has launched at least five major building and renovation projects, including new buildings for biology, chemistry, environmental science, and the Forestry School.<ref name=Wang>{{cite journal |last=Wang |first=Dennis |title=The Story of Science at Yale, Part III: Science at Yale on The Horizon |date=4 November 2012 |journal=Yale Scientific |url=http://www.yalescientific.org/2012/11/the-story-of-science-at-yale-part-iii-science-at-yale-on-the-horizon/ |accessdate=2 March 2014 |archive-date=20 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141120042647/http://www.yalescientific.org/2012/11/the-story-of-science-at-yale-part-iii-science-at-yale-on-the-horizon/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
{{wide image|Yale_Science_Hill.jpg|850px|align-cap=center|Aerial view of Science Hill from the [[Whitney Avenue]] side (west) in 2011. [[Hillhouse Avenue]] begins middle left; a portion of the [[Winchester Repeating Arms Company|Winchester Repeating Arms Factory]] is at top right.}}

== University organizations and departments ==
{{See also|Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences|Yale School of Forestry & Environmental Studies}}
The departments of the [[Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences|Graduate School of Arts and Sciences]] with facilities on Science Hill are: Astronomy; Chemistry; Ecology and Evolutionary Biology; Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry; Molecular, Cellular and Developmental Biology; Geology & Geophysics; [[Yale Department of Physics|Physics]], and Applied Physics. Some biology faculty have joint appointments in the [[Yale School of Medicine]] and have laboratory space within the medical campus.

Most offices and laboratories of the Yale School of Forestry are housed on Science Hill, with a few to its north at [[Marsh Hall (Yale University)|Marsh Hall]]. The school first came to Science Hill in 1924 with the completion of Sage Hall as its new main building.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sage Hall: The New Home of the Yale School of Forestry |periodical=Yale Forest School News |volume=12 |issue=2 |date=April 1924 |publisher=Yale Forest School Alumni Association |pages=19–20}}</ref> In 2008, the school opened Kroon Hall adjacent to Sage. The school also occupies several former mansions at the top of Science Hill.

Connecticut's largest natural history museum, the [[Peabody Museum of Natural History]], relocated from downtown New Haven to the southeastern corner of Science Hill in 1925. The museum is Yale's main repository of scientific collections, including fossils, minerals, archeological artifacts, and animal specimens. As its collections have grown, they have been shifted among at least five science hill buildings, and are currently housed in the museum and the adjacent Kline Geology Laboratory and Environmental Science Center.<ref name="ESC">{{cite web |title=Building for the Future: Care and Conservation of the Peabody Collections |publisher=Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History |url=https://peabody.yale.edu/collections/esc-history |accessdate=22 February 2014}}</ref> The museum also hosts permanent and rotating exhibitions for visitors.

Two facilities of the [[Yale University Library]] are located on Science Hill. The Center for Science & Social Science Information, formerly the Kline Science Library, is housed in the lower levels of Kline Biology Tower, and a geology library resides in Kline Geology Laboratory.

The [[Yale Sustainable Food Project]] is housed in a mansion at the top of the hill and possesses a farm across the street.

== Architecture and art ==

The dominant architectural styles of Science Hill are Gothic revival and mid-century modernist. Later buildings, like the Environmental Science Center and the Bass Center, have attempted to harmonize these earlier styles.<ref name="Fellman 1993">{{cite news |last=Fellman |first=Bruce |title=The Science of Togetherness |magazine=Yale Alumni Magazine |date=October 1993 |url=http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/93_10/science.html |accessdate=2 March 2014 |archive-date=7 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407094051/http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/93_10/science.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Fellman 2002">{{cite news |last=Fellman |first=Bruce |title=Designed for Science |magazine=Yale Alumni Magazine |date=May 2002 |url=http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/02_05/science.html |accessdate=22 February 2014 |archive-date=7 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407094152/http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/02_05/science.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Several buildings are recognized as important architectural monuments, most notably Eero Saarinen's Ingalls Rink and Philip Johnson's Kline Biology Tower.<ref name=Carley /><ref>{{cite news |last=North Reiss |first=Gwen |title=Modernist Living: A Primer |newspaper=The New York Times |date=6 February 2005 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/02/06/nyregion/thecity/06CONN.html |accessdate=23 February 2014}}</ref><ref name="Pinnell">{{cite book |last=Pinnell |first=Patrick |title=The Campus Guide: Yale University |publisher=Princeton Architectural Press |location=Princeton, NJ |year=1999 |edition=1st |isbn=9781568981673}}</ref>{{rp|157–8, 164–5}}

For most of its history, Science Hill has been criticized for its lack of site planning.<ref name=Carley />{{rp|54}} Architectural historian [[Elizabeth Mills Brown]] appraised its 1960s incarnation as Yale's "most poorly integrated, inefficient, and incoherent complex," observing that undeveloped land had offered too much freedom to plan comprehensively.<ref name="Mills Brown" />{{rp|144}} More recently, a campus plan commissioned by the university articulated similar concerns, calling the area "an ill-defined and unattractive pedestrian environment" lacking a "sense of place and focus."<ref>{{cite book |title=A Framework for Campus Planning |author=Cooper, Robertson & Partners |author-link=Cooper, Robertson & Partners |date=April 2000 |url=http://www.yale.edu/about/YALEFRMW.pdf |accessdate=22 February 2014 |page=78 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070615013057/https://www.yale.edu/about/YALEFRMW.pdf |archivedate=15 June 2007 }}</ref> Since 2000, Yale has invested significant resources in improving buildings and connecting areas within Science Hill.<ref name=Arenson /><ref>{{cite news |last=Alden Branch |first=Mark |title=Framing the Future |date=Summer 2000 |magazine=Yale Alumni Magazine |url=http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/00_07/campus_plan.html |accessdate=22 February 2014 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304051028/http://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/00_07/campus_plan.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Several sculptures decorate the hillside. To commemorate his work to found the Sheffield Scientific School, a statue of Benjamin Silliman cast by [[John Ferguson Weir]] resides outside the Sterling Chemistry Laboratory.<ref>{{cite book |last=Falhman |first=Betsy |title=John Fergueson Weir: The Labor of Art |year=1997 |publisher=University of Delaware Press |location=Newark, DE |isbn=9780874136029 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/johnfergusonweir0000fahl/page/154 154–155] |url=https://archive.org/details/johnfergusonweir0000fahl/page/154 }}</ref> A [[Roy Lichtenstein]] sculpture entitled "Modern Head" was placed at the base of Science Hill, near Hillhouse Avenue, in 1993.<ref>{{cite web |title=Public art at Yale - Modern Head |publisher=Yale University |url=http://www.yale.edu/publicart/modernhead.html |accessdate=16 February 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205111946/http://www.yale.edu/publicart/modernhead.html |archivedate=5 December 2014 }}</ref>

'''Davenport College''' (colloquially referred to as '''D'port''') is one of the fourteen [[residential colleges of Yale University]]. Its buildings were completed in 1933<ref>{{cite book|last=Pierson|first=George|title=Yale: the University College, 1921-1937, Volume 2|year=1955|publisher=Yale University Press|pages=636}}</ref>  mainly in the [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] style but with a [[gothic architecture|gothic]] [[façade]] along York Street. The college was named for [[John Davenport (clergyman)|John Davenport]], who founded [[Yale University|Yale]]'s home city of [[New Haven, Connecticut]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Seymour|first=Charles|title=The Yale Residential Colleges|year=1933|publisher=Yale University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://davenport.yale.edu/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100802125857/http://www.yale.edu/davenport/|title=Welcome | Davenport College|archivedate=August 2, 2010|website=davenport.yale.edu|url-status=dead}}</ref>  An extensive renovation of the college's buildings occurred during the 2004–2005 academic year as part of Yale's comprehensive building renovation project. Davenport College has an unofficial rivalry with adjoining [[Pierson College]].

==Namesake==
{{Main|John Davenport (minister)}}
John Davenport was born in 1597 to draper and Mayor of Coventry Henry Davenport and Winifred Barnaby.  He attended [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]] for three years starting in 1613 before leaving without a degree.  He returned to Oxford to finish his MA and [[Bachelor of Divinity]] after serving as the chaplain of [[Hylton Castle|Hilton Castle]] and vicar of [[St. Stephen Coleman Street|St. Stephen's Church]] in London.  In 1633 he resigned from the Church of England after several disputes with the senior clergy.

In 1638 he sailed to North America with his congregation and a [[land patent|patent]] for a [[Massachusetts Bay Colony|colony in Massachusetts]]. One year later he co-founded the city of New Haven with [[Theophilus Eaton]] and served as its burgess until his departure to Boston 30 years later. Beginning in the 1640s, Davenport advocated for the creation of a college near the [[New Haven Green]], a vision realized by [[Yale College]] some fifty years after his death.  He is also credited with co-founding the nearby [[Hopkins School]].

In 1668, Davenport left New Haven to serve as the pastor of the [[First Church in Boston]].  His invitation to that position was not without opposition due to his strict Puritan values, especially regarding infant baptism.  Davenport died of [[apoplexy]] less than two years later.

==Buildings and architecture==
===The College===
[[File:Dport.jpg|thumb|250px|Upper Courtyard viewed from the Crosspiece. [[Harkness Tower]] can be seen in the background]]
Davenport College was, like many of Yale's residential colleges, designed by [[James Gamble Rogers]]. It has two distinct styles of architecture: the York Street facade is constructed from [[gothic architecture|gothically-detailed]] sandstone while the remainder of the college has been built in the red-brick [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] style of the colonial era.<ref>{{cite news|last=Brock|first=H.I.|title=OLD BECOMES NEW AT YALE AND HARVARD|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1933/11/19/archives/old-becomes-new-at-yale-and-harvard-the-intimate-life-of-the-early.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=November 19, 1933}}</ref>  This "hybridization" is meant to complement the monumental gothic streetscape of York Street, on which the western façades of the [[Branford College|Branford]] and [[Saybrook College]] complex along with [[Jonathan Edwards College]] stand opposite the gothic-inspired [[Yale Daily News]] building and University Theater. On the inner, Georgian face, the college entrance has an adaptation of the eastern façade of the [[Old State House (Boston)|original Massachusetts Statehouse]], in which the British imperial lion and unicorn have been replaced by a pair of [[Yale (mythical creature)|yales]]. The inner face was featured in the 2008 movie [[The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2]].

[[File:Davenport College Upper Courtyard-opposing view.JPG|thumb|Davenport College, Upper Courtyard viewed from York St. Gate.]]
The enclosed space of Davenport College features three courtyards: Kumble Court (usually referred to as the "upper courtyard"), the lower courtyard and a recently created stone courtyard in front of the dean's suite, the result of the annexation of the former [[Yale Record]] building during the 2004–2005 renovations. A half-story terrace and two house-like residential units (one dubbed "The Cottage") flank the upper courtyard to the north. Traditionally, the college's sophomores live in the suites bordering the lower courtyard, while most of the juniors and seniors of the College live around the upper courtyard.

Separating the two main courtyards is the Crosspiece, housing both the Dean's and Head's Offices and a classroom space as well as carrels and reading rooms extending from the college's Spitzer Library. The Crosspiece formerly held a second library in the top floor which has since been converted to student housing, with the book holdings moved into the expanded Library. Indoor spaces of architectural note include the Davenport Common Room, the aforementioned Spitzer Library and the Dining Hall. The Dining Hall's walls are adorned with a two-panel portrait showcasing the diversity of the college's staff and students.<ref>{{Cite web|first=Brianna|last=Wu|date=April 23, 2018|title=Davenport unveils dining hall portrait|url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2018/04/23/davenport-unveils-dining-hall-portrait/|access-date=January 27, 2021|website=yaledailynews.com|language=en}}</ref> A [[Waterford crystal]] chandelier hangs from the dining hall's ceiling.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Davenport |url=https://hospitality.yale.edu/residential-dining/davenport|access-date=June 28, 2021|website=hospitality.yale.edu}}</ref>

The student buttery, or "The Dive", is the snack shop. An entertainment center—and game room is nearby. The Davenport basement also includes a [[Letterpress|letterpress print-shop]], a pottery studio, a digital media arts center, a dance studio, and a small theater with stadium seating. These are all shared with students in [[Pierson College|Pierson]]. Davenport students also have access to shared facilities on the Pierson side of the basement, including music practice rooms and an exercise room containing treadmills, ellipticals, and free weights.

[[File:Welchhallold.jpg|thumb|left|220px|Welch Hall circa 1895. Until 2024, Davenport freshmen lived in Welch. From ''Yale Yarns: Sketches of Life at Yale University'' by John Seymour Wood.  (New York: The Knickerbocker Press, 1895.)]]

===Freshman housing===
Davenport College freshmen live on the [[Old Campus]] with the rest of their Yale College class, with the exception of students from [[Silliman College|Silliman]], [[Timothy Dwight College|Timothy Dwight]], [[Pauli Murray College|Pauli Murray]], and [[Franklin College (Yale University)|Benjamin Franklin]]. Currently, Davenport College, along with [[Grace Hopper College]] freshmen live in [[Lanman Wright Hall (Yale)|Lanman Wright Hall]], also known as "LDub", which is located next to Daniels Gate on Elm Street.  Lanman Wright is known for being the "worst accommodation at Yale", with cramped bunk beds and tight living quarters being the norm.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2023/02/24/the-good-fortune-of-living-in-lanman-wright-hall/|title=The Good Fortune of Living in Lanman Wright Hall - Yale Daily News|first=Sahar|last=Tartak|website=yaledailynews.com}}</ref>

== History ==

Under the Yale College policy that let incoming students express a residential college preference, Davenport developed a reputation for attracting athletic, upper-class elites until the policy ended with the class of 1958.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kelley |first1=Brooks Mather |title=[[Yale: A History]] |date=1974 |language=English |isbn=978-0-300-01636-9 |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |oclc=810552  |page=448 }}</ref>

In 2022, Gonzalez succeeded [[John Fabian Witt]] as head of Davenport College, making her the first Black woman to serve as head of college in Yale's history.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Cook |first1=Sarah |last2=Porayouw |first2=William |date=2022-04-22 |title=Anjelica Gonzalez and Paul North named Davenport and JE heads of college  |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2022/04/22/anjelica-gonzalez-and-paul-north-named-davenport-and-je-heads-of-college-%ef%bf%bc/ |access-date=2022-04-26 |website=Yale Daily News |language=en}}</ref>

==Mascot==
<!-- Commented out because image was deleted: [[File:Davenport Gnome.jpg|thumb|right|150px|The D'port Gnome.]] -->
For a while after Davenport College's inception into the Yale residential college system, students were known as "Hybrids," a reference to the hybrid style of the college's architecture. While the nickname appeared in a few official publications in the 1970s, it was no longer used by either Davenporters or their rivals.  Davenport students were without a title or figure to rally behind.

In 1998, then junior Thomas Shaw, upon returning from a semester of mountaineering, brought back from the [[Redwood Empire|California Redwood country]] a five-and-a-half foot tall, 400 pound carved wooden [[gnome]] as a gift to the college. The gnome, with its green painted shirt and yellow pants, quickly developed a following in the Davenport community, and was soon proudly adopted as the college's official [[mascot]].

The gnome was first placed in the college's courtyard, but after repeated theft by neighbor and unofficial Davenport rival [[Pierson College|Pierson]], the gnome was relocated inside. It was in the entrance of the administrative offices in Crosspiece for the first semester of the 2005–2006 school year, but was moved to the Davenport Dining Hall. In April 2011, Davenport students stopped a group of Piersonites from the most recent attempt at stealing the gnome. The gnome was successfully rescued and taken to its home in the Davenport Dining Hall.<ref>{{cite web|last=Daniel|first=Daniel|title=Davenport's gnome rescued from Piersonites|url=http://www.yaledailynews.com/news/2011/apr/23/davenports-gnome-rescued-piersonites/|publisher=Yale Daily News|access-date=April 26, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110508150849/http://www.yaledailynews.com/news/2011/apr/23/davenports-gnome-rescued-piersonites/|archive-date=May 8, 2011}}</ref>

==Intramurals==
Davenport College has competed for the Tyng Cup, winning the championship six times, most recently in 2014.<ref name="undergradims">{{cite web|url=https://recreation.yale.edu/undergradims|title=Intramurals: Undergraduate|publisher=Yale University|access-date=February 1, 2026}}</ref> The college's ice hockey team has won 16 championships, most recently in 1997.{{citation needed|date = July 2011}}  Davenport has won championships in table tennis, golf, bowling, men's volleyball, swimming, softball, and track and field.{{citation needed|date = July 2011}}

'''Pierson College''' is a [[Residential colleges of Yale University|residential college]] at [[Yale University]] in [[New Haven, Connecticut|New Haven]], [[Connecticut]]. Opened in 1933, it is named for [[Abraham Pierson]], a founder and the first [[Rector (academia)|rector]] of the Collegiate School, the college later known as Yale. With just under 500 undergraduate members, Pierson is the largest of Yale's residential colleges by number of students.

{{TOC limit|3}}

==History==
[[File:Pierson College from the sky.jpg|thumb|200px|left|The college's building and grounds from above, with Davenport College (at top)]]
Yale built the Pierson College buildings in the [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] or "Georgian Revival" architectural style.  These include a prominent tower, inspired by that of Philadelphia's [[Independence Hall]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Elizabeth |last=Mills Brown |title=New Haven, a Guide to Architecture and Urban Design |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |year=1976 |page=126 |isbn=0300019939 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9no2loQlCeEC&q=pierson+college+architect+gamble+rogers+georgian&pg=PA126 |access-date=2012-05-28}}</ref>  It is one of the eight original residential colleges bequeathed by [[Edward Harkness]] and designed by [[James Gamble Rogers]].

Pierson College's first [[Master (college)|master]] was [[Alan Valentine]], then in 1935 international relations scholar [[Arnold Wolfers]] took over the role,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1935/02/11/88611835.html | title=Heads Pierson College | newspaper=The New York Times | date=February 11, 1935 | page=17}}</ref> one he held until 1949.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1968/07/17/archives/arnold-wolfers-historian-dead-held-international-relations.html | title=Arnold Wolfers, Historian, Dead: Held International Relations Professorship at Yale | newspaper=The New York Times | date= July 17, 1968 | page=43}}</ref> Wolfers and his wife Doris made the Master's House at Pierson a center for entertaining on the campus second only to the house of the president of the university.  Among those they hosted where diplomats who visited the campus.<ref>{{cite book | first=Robin W. | last=Winks | title=Cloak & Gown: Scholars in the Secret War, 1939–1961 | publisher=William Morrow and Company | location=New York | year=1987 | pages=40–41}}</ref>

During World War II, Wolfers played a significant role in recruiting students into the intelligence services such as the OSS, and overall a disproportionate number of intelligence workers came from Pierson College.  In addition to Wolfers, other Pierson fellows who did recruiting included [[Wallace Notestein]] and [[C. Bradford Welles]]. Pierson College residents who later became intelligence figures included future CIA counterintelligence chief [[James Jesus Angleton]], who often spent time in Wolfers' living room listening to poets such as [[Robert Frost]] that Wolfers brought in to read.  Other attendees to these sessions included a future U.S. Poet Laureate, [[Reed Whittemore]].<ref>{{cite book | first=Robin W. | last=Winks | title=Cloak & Gown: Scholars in the Secret War, 1939–1961 | publisher=William Morrow and Company | location=New York | year=1987 | pages=38–40, 51, 11th page of plates following p. 230, 336}}</ref>

In 2004, Yale completed a year long renovation of Pierson as part of a campaign to rehabilitate all twelve colleges. Major changes included the reconfiguration of existing suites and rooms, the move of the "Dean's" office, the addition of a new residential building, Upper Court.  Most significantly, the renovation joined the basements of Pierson its adjacent and [[college rivalry|rival]] residential college, [[Davenport College|Davenport]], giving the colleges common facilities.

The courtyard was home to [[George Rickey]]'s [[kinetic sculpture]], "Two Planes Vertical—Horizontal II" for many years, but the sculpture has now been moved to the courtyard of the [[Yale University Art Gallery]].

==Namesake==
{{main article|Abraham Pierson}}

Abraham Pierson was born in [[Southampton]], [[Long Island]] in 1646 and was an early student at [[Harvard College]]. After many years as a Congregational minister in [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]], [[New Jersey]], he assumed the [[pulpit]] in [[Killingworth, Connecticut]] in 1694. While presiding there, he and five other ministers established the [[List of colonial colleges|third college]] in the [[Thirteen Colonies|American colonies]], the Collegiate School, in 1701.<ref name="Mather Kelly">{{cite book |first=Brooks |last=Mather Kelly |title=Yale: A History |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |year=1978}}</ref> Pierson was elected its first [[Rector (academia)|rector]], but unable to leave his position in Killingworth, he taught courses from his parsonage in present-day [[Clinton, Connecticut|Clinton]]. Pierson died in his sixth year as Yale's rector, in 1707.

A statue of Pierson stands on Yale's [[Old Campus]]. Since there are no known portraits of Pierson, the statue is an "imaginative recreation."<ref name="Mather Kelly" />

==Student life==
[[File:Lanman Wright courtyard elevated.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Lanman-Wright Hall]]
Pierson freshmen are currently housed in Vanderbilt Hall on [[Old Campus]].

Pierson has been traditionally renowned for its thriving social life and once had the reputation of consistently trailing other Yale residential colleges in academic rankings. In fact, Pierson's rallying cry at one time was, "Tyng, Tang, and GPA," reflecting Pierson's reputation for winning Yale intramural sports (Tyng), an annual drinking competition among the residential colleges (Tang), and having the lowest average GPA of all the residential colleges.  In 2004, 2018, and 2021, however, Pierson has been awarded the Gimbel Cup<ref>{{cite web | url=https://secretary.yale.edu/services-resources/lectureships-fellowships-and-prizes/residential-prizes?field_residential_college_tid=All | title=Residential College Prizes | Office of the Secretary and Vice President for University Life }}</ref> for highest average GPA at Yale.  In light of new Connecticut alcohol laws, Dean Amerigo Fabbri has cracked down on events such as Tuesday Night Club (TNC), founded in 1981, restricting the event to Pierson seniors. However, in 2006, Pierson students were able to organize a successful Inferno, the traditional Pierson Halloween party.  TNC was traditionally held in the "Lower Courtyard" of Pierson.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=alnup81pmkAC&q=%22slave+quarters%22+pierson&pg=PA67 |title=The Campus Guide: Yale University - Patrick Pinnell - Google Books |date= June 1999|isbn=9781568981673 |access-date=2012-05-28|last1=Pinnell |first1=Patrick |publisher=Princeton Architectural Press }}</ref> Lower Courtyard housing is generally occupied by seniors.<ref name="piersoncollege1">{{cite web |title=Florida Real Estate | Destin Hotel | Orlando Vacation Home at Piersoncollege.com |url=http://www.piersoncollege.com/cgi-bin/index.cgi?action=viewnews&id=11 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111004042915/http://www.piersoncollege.com/cgi-bin/index.cgi?action=viewnews&id=11 |archive-date=2011-10-04 |access-date=2012-05-28 |publisher=Pierson College}}</ref>

Another Pierson tradition is Pierson Day, which typically falls on the last day of classes of the academic year.  On Pierson Day, the Head of Pierson College wrestles another College Head, student, or other willing opponent in a ring filled with yellow [[jello]].

Pierson achieved world renown in 1977 as a result of the still-famous television broadcast of its [[Bladderball]] 'victory'.{{citation needed|date=July 2014}} Pierson's most storied tradition is the theft of Davenport College's gnome mascot. Pierson's famous "fight song," heard annually at "the Game" between the Yale and Harvard football teams, starts off with:  "'P' is for the 'P' in Pierson College; 'I' is for the 'I' in Pierson College," and continues in predictable fashion.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.yaleherald.com/archive/frosh/1999/here/p04colleges.html |title=Residential colleges: not just dorms, but microcosms of Yale's community | Summer 1999 |publisher=Yaleherald.com |access-date=2012-05-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120212234653/http://www.yaleherald.com/archive/frosh/1999/here/p04colleges.html |archive-date=2012-02-12 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
[[File:Quincy Porter Pierson College 1961.jpg|thumb|right|[[Quincy Porter]] at Pierson in 1961]]
Among the activities for which Pierson is known is the Pierson Press, one of the most active of Yale's many traditional [[letterpress]] print shops. It was founded over half a century ago and nurtured by a succession of Pierson Heads including [[John Hersey]], [[Quincy Porter]], [[Gaddis Smith]], and Harvey Goldblatt. For many years the Press was located in a converted squash court in Pierson Tower, designed by [[Charles Willard Moore]] of the Yale School of Architecture. During the renovation of the college in 2004, it was relocated to enhanced facilities in the basement, where it now shares space with the Davenport Press in a greatly expanded Book Arts Center that includes half a dozen presses, over 1000 cases of hand type, a book bindery, paper mill and more. Over 75 Pierson and Davenport students attended the college's rigorous Apprentice Course during the Fall of 2005.

The basement of Pierson is also home to the Pierson [[Buttery (shop)|Buttery]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://piersonbuttery.com |title=See What's Available and Place an Order |publisher=Piersonbuttery.com |access-date=2012-05-28 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622234345/http://www.piersonbuttery.com/ |archive-date=2012-06-22 }}</ref> The Buttery  is run by students and offers a variety of late night food options that can be [https://web.archive.org/web/20120331022932/http://www.piersonbuttery.com/ ordered online]. In the Spring of 2007, Pierson won the annual Freshmen Olympics, held on Old Campus. The Class of 2010 beat the eleven other residential colleges in Pierson's first ever Freshman Olympics victory. Since then, Pierson has won the Freshman Olympics several times, most recently in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://yaledailynews.com/blog/2014/04/07/pierson-freshmen-emerge-victorious-2/|title=Pierson freshmen emerge victorious|date=7 April 2014}}</ref>

Pierson's Fellowship, consisting of both faculty members and distinguished outside Associate Fellows, is one of the most active at Yale. The Fellows meet twice monthly during the academic year, generously support undergraduate activities in the college, including social events such as the annual Pierson Inferno at Halloween. Throughout its history, the group has consisted of a diverse and dignified range of members, from poet [[Robert Frost]] to actor [[George Takei]] (Sulu of Star Trek fame) to [[G. D. Mostow]] the [[mathematician]] of [[Mostow rigidity theorem]] fame and [[Calvin Hill]], [[NFL]] Rookie of the Year and multiple [[Pro Bowl]] selectee.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aeispeakers.com/speakerbio.php?SpeakerID=501|title=We are sorry, that speaker is no longer with us}}</ref>

Pierson was home to one of the longest serving Yale residential college deans, Dean Christa Dove '76 MPhil.  Within the Residential College system at Yale, deanships normally last only a few years. Dove, however, was Dean of Pierson College for 22 years, from 1983 to 2005.<ref>{{cite web|author=Yale Alumni Publications, Inc. |url=http://archive.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/2004_11/milestones.html |title=Milestones |publisher=Yale Alumni Magazine |access-date=2013-08-30}}</ref>

[[File:Pierson Library.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Pierson library after 2004 renovation]]
The renovation of 2003-04 was extensive, and included the reconfiguration of student suites, student activities areas, and dining facilities; new bathrooms, new interior finishes and lighting; additional student rooms in a new Upper Court building; complete replacement of all mechanical and electrical systems; new security, fire protection, and information technology systems; new elevators, ramps, and other enhancements to accessibility; and repairs to windows, masonry, roofs, and gutters.<ref name="yaleherald1">[http://www.yaleherald.com/article.php?Article=2517] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061111225340/http://www.yaleherald.com/article.php?Article=2517|date=November 11, 2006}}</ref> The renovation also included enlarging the library and adding a mezzanine level computer cluster.<ref name="yaleherald1"/> The completion of the additional building,  called "Upper Court", increased Pierson College's dorm space capacity from 264 to 310.<ref name="yaleherald1"/> During the renovation, students who would otherwise live in Pierson College, lived in what is called "Swing Space," dormitories located near [[Payne Whitney Gymnasium]] that resemble a cheap hotel and do not include a dining hall.<ref name="yaleherald1"/>

A number of the songs from [[Dirty Projectors]]' Don Henley and Hernán Cortés infused glitch-opera, [[The Getty Address]], were recorded in Pierson College, as [[Dave Longstreth]] was a student at Yale.

Pierson's sister college is [[Lowell House]] at [[Harvard University]].

The inaugural Pierson College all-alumni reunion was recently held in New Haven from February 15–17, 2013, coinciding with the 80th year of the college's existence.  Notable Pierson alumni in attendance included [[Howard Dean]], PC '71, and [[George Pataki]], PC '67.  Also honored during the celebration were Head of College Harvey Goldblatt, who completed his 19th and final year as Head of Pierson College in May 2013, and Yale's then President-elect (now President) Peter Salovey.

'''Silliman College''' is a [[residential colleges of Yale University|residential college]] at [[Yale University]] in [[New Haven, Connecticut]]. The college is named for [[Benjamin Silliman]], the first science professor at Yale.<ref name="History Silliman College">{{Cite web |title=History {{!}} Silliman College |url=https://silliman.yalecollege.yale.edu/about-silliman/history |access-date=2025-04-20 |website=silliman.yalecollege.yale.edu}}</ref> It opened in September 1940 as the last of the original ten residential colleges, and contains buildings constructed as early as 1901.

Silliman is Yale's largest residential college by its footprint, occupying most of a city block.<ref name="Pinnell"/> Due to its size, the college is able to house its first-year students in the college instead of on Yale's [[Old Campus]]. The college's architecture is varied: though architect Otto Eggers completed most of the college with [[Georgian Revival architecture|Georgian]] buildings, the college also incorporates two early-20th century buildings in the [[Neo-Renaissance|French Renaissance]] and [[Gothic Revival]] styles.

The college has links to [[Harvard]]'s [[Pforzheimer House]] and [[Dudley House (Harvard College)|Dudley House]], as well as [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] and [[Brasenose College, Oxford]]. Its rival college at Yale is [[Timothy Dwight College]], located directly across Temple Street.

==History==
[[File:Byers Hall and new Vanderbilt Hall, Yale University, New Haven, Conn.jpg|thumb|250px|Byers Hall and Vanderbilt Hall, then part of the [[Sheffield Scientific School]], now Silliman's main facade.]]
Silliman College is located on the lands of the [[Quinnipiac]] people.<ref name="History Silliman College"/> The oldest known non-Indigenous settlement at the college's current site was the farm of Robert Newman, whose barn hosted the meeting that incorporated the Colony of New Haven in 1639.<ref name="Pinnell">{{cite book |last=Pinnell |first=Patrick |title=The Campus Guide: Yale University |date=1999 |pages=116–17 |publisher=Princeton University Press |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=alnup81pmkAC&pg=PA116 |access-date=April 7, 2015|isbn=9781568981673 }}</ref> The tract later became one of the blocks of New Haven's original nine-square city plan. Yale's first buildings on the site were for the [[Sheffield Scientific School]]. Byers Hall, a three-story building of [[Indiana limestone]], was built in 1903 and designed by [[Hiss and Weekes]] architects in the [[Neo-Renaissance|modified French Renaissance Style]]. The Vanderbilt-Sheffield dormitory, a five-story building of the same material, was built between 1903 and 1906 by architect [[Charles C. Haight]] in the [[Gothic Revival|Gothic Revival style]].

[[File:HABS Northeast elevation, Noah Webster House, Temple & Grove Streets, New Haven, Conn.jpg|thumb|250px|right|The Noah Webster House, on the corner of Grove St and Temple St, before its removal]]
In 1936, the university demolished the block of university buildings and houses that stood at the site, retaining only Van-Sheff, Byers Hall, and the adjacent [[St. Anthony Hall]] society building. The New Haven home of [[Noah Webster]], occupied by its namesake from 1822 to 1843, was one of the structures scheduled for demolition. During ensuing controversy over the home's preservation, [[Henry Ford]] purchased the building and had it disassembled and re-erected at [[Greenfield Village]] in [[Dearborn, Michigan]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Noah Webster House, New Haven, Connecticut |date=1936 |website=Historical American Buildings Survey |publisher=Library of Congress |url=http://lcweb2.loc.gov/master/pnp/habshaer/ct/ct0100/ct0188/data/ct0188data.pdf |access-date=April 7, 2015}}</ref> A plaque now marks the site of the Webster House on the college's northeast corner.<ref name="Pinnell"/>

[[File:Silliman College, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut. Master's house from quadrangle.jpg|thumb|250px|right|House of the Silliman Master, a Georgian Revival design by Otto Eggers]]
The "Quadrangle Plan," primarily funded by [[Edward Harkness]], opened nine residential colleges for Yale between 1933 and 1934. Eight colleges were intended for [[Yale College]], and two further for the Scientific School, one of which would be funded by [[Frederick W. Vanderbilt]]. This tenth college was planned by 1931, when [[Charles Hyde Warren]] was appointed as a college master, and named for [[Benjamin Silliman]] in 1933. Warren, also [[Sterling Professor|Sterling Professor of Geology]] and Dean of the Sheffield Scientific School, wrote a biography of Silliman but only retained his appointment until 1938, two years before the college's opening. Otto Eggers of [[Eggers & Higgins]], previously a draftsman for [[John Russell Pope]]'s buildings at Yale, was selected as the college's architect.<ref name="Pinnell"/> Eggers' design preserved Van Sheff, reconstructed the interior of Byers Hall, and created a quadrangle of Georgian buildings to complete the college and harmonize it with the adjacent [[Timothy Dwight College]], established six years earlier.

When the college opened in 1940, philosopher [[F. S. C. Northrop]] was appointed its master.

Under the Yale College policy that let incoming students express a residential college preference, Silliman developed a reputation for attracting engineers until the policy ended with the class of 1958.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kelley |first1=Brooks Mather |title=[[Yale: A History]] |date=1974 |language=English |isbn=978-0-300-01636-9 |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |oclc=810552  |page=448 }}</ref>

== Shield and mascot ==
Silliman College's shield has a white background, three curving red lines emerging from near the bottom of the shield (representing salamander tails), and a green crossing bar containing three acorns. In heraldic terms, the shield is described as "Arms: Argent, three piles wavy gules, on a fess vert three acorns or."  The colors represent the four ancient elements: red for fire, white for air and water, and green for earth. The acorns are an element taken from the family arms of [[Frederick Vanderbilt]], 1876, who funded the college's construction.

The college's mascot is the salamander. Students in the college refer to themselves as Sillimanders.

==Facilities==
The college courtyard, which covers almost an entire city block, is the largest enclosed courtyard at Yale and is one of the glories of the old college. Students can be seen playing various sports or lounging in the sun. Because of the size of the courtyard, sports such as spikeball, wiffle ball, football, and frisbee are often enjoyed.

Special facilities within Silliman include Yale's only undergraduate art gallery, called Maya's Room (named for Maya Tanaka Hanway, '83), a big-screen movie theater (Silliflicks), a dance studio, a half-court basketball facility called the Sillidome, computing facilities, a student kitchen, multiple music practice rooms, and a state-of-the-art<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sillimancollege.org/modules/tinycontent/index.php?id=36 |title=Silliman College - Silliman Pages |access-date=October 17, 2005 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051230071504/http://www.sillimancollege.org/modules/tinycontent/index.php?id=36 |archive-date=December 30, 2005 }}</ref> sound recording studio. The college's library, located in the third floor of Byers Hall, is commonly referred to as the Sillibrary. The Buttery, a student-run eatery in the basement that serves greasy goodness on weekday nights, is designed in the style of the 1950s and its surrounding area includes games such as ping pong, air hockey, and pool

==College administrators and student representatives==
The Head of College for Silliman is Arielle Baskin-Sommers,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cook |first=Sarah |date=2023-03-08 |title=Arielle Baskin-Sommers announced as head of Silliman |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2023/03/07/arielle-baskin-sommers-announced-as-head-of-silliman/ |access-date=2025-04-19 |website=Yale Daily News |language=en}}</ref> an associate professor of psychology and of psychiatry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arielle Baskin-Sommers {{!}} Department of Psychology |url=https://psychology.yale.edu/people/arielle-baskin-sommers |access-date=2025-04-19 |website=psychology.yale.edu |language=en}}</ref> She was appointed to her current role in March 2023, succeeding the previous Head of college [[Laurie R. Santos]].

The current Residential College Dean of Silliman is Matthew Newman.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Matt Newman Residential College Dean Silliman College {{!}} Classics |url=https://silliman.yale.edu/profile/matt-newman |access-date=2026-10-29 |website=silliman.yale.edu |language=en}}</ref> In his capacity as dean, Newman is tasked with advising Silliman students based upon their individual circumstances, both academically and holistically.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dean's Office {{!}} Silliman College |url=https://silliman.yalecollege.yale.edu/deans-office |access-date=2025-04-19 |website=silliman.yalecollege.yale.edu}}</ref>

The Silliman Activities and Administrative Committee (SAAC) collaborates with the Silliman Head of college on arranging Silliman social events and community service projects. The SAAC also serves as a forum for discussion of Silliman issues for college students. The SAAC president for the 2025–2026 academic year is Emma Popowitz whereas the SAAC vice president is Steven Rourick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SAAC {{!}} Silliman College |url=https://silliman.yalecollege.yale.edu/saac |access-date=2025-04-19 |website=silliman.yalecollege.yale.edu}}</ref>

==Renovations==
In August 2007, after three years of on-and-off renovations, students moved back into Silliman College. Students now enjoy a reconfigured dining hall and servery, a stadium-seating movie theater, and a large student activities space that includes a new art gallery, dance studio, gym, basketball court, weight room, buttery, game room, and television entertainment space. The Silliman College courtyard was also restored to its former glory, with new patio spaces, benches, and grass. The renovation cost some $100 million, by far the most spent on any residential college renovation at Yale.<ref>[http://www.yaledailynews.com/articles/view/21987 Yale Daily News - Expansion Projected at $600 Million] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080124143042/http://yaledailynews.com/articles/view/21987 |date=January 24, 2008 }}</ref>

Because of the size of Silliman College, the renovation work on the college was completed in several phases instead of the 15-month renovation completed on other colleges:
* In the summer of 2004, the roof and windows were replaced on the brick section of the college. Extra dormers were also added to the roofs so that student rooms could later be installed in the former attic spaces.
* In the summer of 2005, the Silliman Tower underwent a complete interior renovation.
* The entire college was shut down during the 2006–2007 school year for the rest of the renovation. All students from the college moved into either Swing Space (a new dormitory built especially to house students during college renovations), the Elm Street Annex or into independent off-campus housing until the renovations were completed.
* In 2017, a coffee shop, The Acorn, was added into the fourth floor of Byers Hall.

==Activities and traditions==

===Intramural sports===
Silliman College has won the Tyng Cup (awarded for the best intramural record of Yale's 14 residential colleges) eight times, in 1941, 1943, 1968, 1969, 1972, 2006, 2007, and 2008.<ref>{{cite web|title=Past Tyng Cup Champions by Year|url=https://intramurals.yale.edu/past-tyng-cup-champions|website=Past Tyng Cup Champions|access-date=May 5, 2018|ref=5}}</ref>

== Silliman fame ==
Silliman gained fame when the popular movie ''[[Mona Lisa Smile]]'' featuring [[Julia Roberts]], [[Julia Stiles]] and [[Kirsten Dunst]], was partly filmed in the Silliman College courtyard and common room. The Grove Street facade of Silliman was used to represent Harvard University, and the Wall Street Gate and the common room were used to represent [[Wellesley College]].{{citation needed|date=October 2016}}

'''Berkeley College''' is a [[residential colleges of Yale University|residential college]] at [[Yale University]], opened in 1934. The eighth of Yale's 14 residential colleges, it was named in honor of Bishop [[George Berkeley]] (1685–1753), dean of [[Derry]] and later bishop of [[Cloyne]], in recognition of the assistance in land and books that he gave to Yale in the 18th century. Built on the site of a group of buildings known from the 1890s until 1933 as the '''Berkeley Oval''',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://berkeley.yalecollege.yale.edu | title=History - Berkeley College - Yale University}}</ref> the college was renovated in 1998.  It is distinct for having two courtyards connected by an underground tunnel.

==College life==
{{prose|section|date=May 2024}}
{{Unreferenced section|date=April 2024}}
[[File:Berkeley College (South) at Yale.jpg|thumb|left|The southern portion of Berkeley College]]

*Berkeley freshmen are housed in [[Lanman-Wright Hall]], renovated in 2014.
*Dining Hall: The dining hall is named in honor of Joseph Fogg.  
*Buttery: Currently known as The Coq Pit. Known in the 2000s, 2010s, and early 2020s as Marvin's; known in the 1980s and 1990s as the "Bagel Bar."
*Library: Also known as "Laz," study space named in honor of George Lazarus and Shelly Lazarus.  
*South Court Basement.
*Multipurpose Room: A half-court space to play basketball, it is also frequently used for practicing yoga or student orchestra rehearsals. It can be reserved through the Head's Office.
* North Court Basement: Home to The [[Thomas C. Mendenhall (historian)|Thomas Mendenhall]] Common Room and the Samuel Hemingway Music Room.
* The Swiss Room: A private dining room in the dining hall. Transplanted piece by piece from [[Switzerland]], this 16th-century wooden room has been decorated with [[stained glass]] by [[G. Owen Bonawit]] and is considered priceless.  Access is restricted to fellows and Berkeley events.
* The tunnel: An underground passageway connecting Berkeley's two grand courts, North Court and South Court, which are divided by a grassy area in front of Yale's main library, [[Sterling Memorial Library]]. It stands steps away from the [[Beinecke Library]], the [[Bass Library]], the Commons, and the Old Campus. The tunnel features a variety of student murals on the walls.
*On the wall outside the Head's House that faces [[Sterling Memorial Library]], there is a plaque stating that its location marks the house where [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]] lived.
* The Head's House was named as the Swensen House in 2013 to honor Berkeley Fellow David Swensen's enormous contributions to Yale as the Chief Investment Officer.
* Similar to other residential colleges, Berkeley has its own gym, seminar rooms, and other amenities.

==Traditions==
[[File:Reverend George Berkeley by Alfred C. Hart.jpg|thumb|Reverend George Berkeley by Alfred C. Hart]]

Annual traditions include the Berkeley Birthday Dinner for fellows and seniors, Thunder Brunch, Lunar New Year's Feast, a snowball fight (which pits North Court against South Court), GLO (a blacklight party), and the Bishop Bash, which was founded in the spring of 2002 by Ben Reiter and [[Charles Finch]] under the guidance of the Head's Office.
