Yale Divinity School:
{{Short description|Graduate school of Yale University}} {{Infobox university | name = Yale Divinity School | type = Private | parent = [[Yale University]] | accreditation = [[Association of Theological Schools]] | religious_affiliation = Interdenominational and nonsectarian | endowment = $670 million | students = 287 (2025){{cite web |url=https://www.ats.edu/member-schools/yale-divinity-school|title=Yale Divinity School|work=The Association of Theological Schools}} | image = Yale Divinity School.svg | image_upright = .7 | image_alt = [[Coat of arms]] of the school, containing a book device inscribed with Hebrew letters and cross in front of a red background | caption = [[Coat of arms]] of the school
with the university's ''[[Urim and Thummim|Urim V'Thummim]]'' motto under a [[Celtic cross|cross and halo]] | former_names = Yale School of Religion | motto = Lux et Veritas | motto_eng = Light and Truth | established = {{Start date and age|1822}} | city = [[New Haven, Connecticut]] | country = U.S. | coordinates = {{Coord|41|19|24|N|72|55|17|W|region:US_type:edu|display=title}} | dean = [[Gregory Sterling | Gregory E. Sterling]] | faculty = | mascot = Heavenly Dan | logo = | website = {{url|https://divinity.yale.edu}} }} '''Yale Divinity School''' ('''YDS''') is one of the twelve graduate and professional schools of [[Yale University]] in [[New Haven, Connecticut]]. [[Congregational church|Congregationalist]] [[Theology|theological]] education was the motivation at the founding of Yale, and the professional school has its roots in a Theological Department established in 1822. The school had maintained its own campus, faculty, and degree program since 1869, and it has become more [[Ecumenism|ecumenical]] beginning in the mid-19th century. Since the 1970s, it has been affiliated with the [[Episcopalianism|Episcopal]] [[Berkeley Divinity School]] and has housed the [[Yale Institute of Sacred Music|Institute of Sacred Music]], which offers separate degree programs. In July 2017, a two-year process of formal affiliation was completed, with the addition of [[Andover Newton Seminary at Yale Divinity School|Andover Newton Seminary]] joining the school. Over 40 different denominations are represented at YDS.{{Cite web|title=Admissions FAQ {{!}} Yale Divinity School|url=https://divinity.yale.edu/admissions-aid/admissions-faq|access-date=2021-03-18|website=divinity.yale.edu}} As of 2026, Yale Divinity School is the most selective divinity school in the world.{{Cite web |title=A Message from the Dean < Yale University |url=https://catalog.yale.edu/div/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=catalog.yale.edu}} ==History== [[File:Divinity College at Yale before 1870, Memories of Yale life and men, 1854-1899 (1903).jpg|thumb|200px|The Divinity College dormitory on the [[Old Campus (Yale University)|Old Campus]], completed in 1836]] Theological education was the earliest academic purpose of Yale University. When [[Yale College]] was founded in 1701, it was as a college of religious training for [[Congregationalist]] ministers in [[Connecticut Colony]], designated in its charter as a school "wherein Youth may be instructed in the Arts & Sciences who through the blessing of Almighty God may be fitted for Publick employment both in Church & Civil State." A professorship of divinity was established in 1746. In 1817, the occupant of the divinity chair, [[Eleazar Thompson Fitch]], supported a student request to endow a theological curriculum, and five years later a separate {{nowrap|'''Yale Theological Seminary'''}}{{citation |title=History of Higher Education Annual: 1997 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=vgQaGJt9OTQC&pg=PA94 94] }}. was founded by the [[Yale Corporation]].{{cite book |title=A General Catalogue of the Divinity School of Yale College: A Brief Biographical Record of Its Members in The First Half Century of Its Existence as A Distinct Department |url=https://archive.org/details/generalcatalogue00yalerich |publisher=Tuttle, Morehouse, & Taylor |year=1873 |location=New Haven}} In the same motion, [[Second Great Awakening]] theologian [[Nathaniel William Taylor]] was appointed to become the first Dwight Professor of Didactic Theology.{{cite web |title=Yale Divinity School Milestones, 1822-2012 |publisher=Yale University Library |date=23 October 2012 |url=http://divinity-adhoc.library.yale.edu/Exhibits/YDSMilestones.htm |access-date=16 November 2015}} Taylor was considered the "central figure" in the school's founding, and he was joined in 1826 by [[Josiah Willard Gibbs, Sr.]], a scholar of sacred languages and lexicographer [[Chauncey A. Goodrich]] in 1839. A dedicated student dormitory, Divinity College, was completed on the college's [[Old Campus (Yale University)|Old Campus]] in 1836, but the department had no permanent classrooms or offices until several years after the end of the [[American Civil War]]. [[File:Old Divinity School, Yale University, New Haven, Conn.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Divinity Hall, occupied from 1870 to 1931, viewed from the [[New Haven Green]].]] After a significant period of enrollment decline, the school began fundraising from alumni for new faculty and facilities. Divinity Hall was constructed on the present-day site of [[Calhoun College|Grace Hopper College]] between 1869 and 1871, featuring two classroom wings and a chapel. Around the time of the new campus' construction came the arrival of new faculty, including [[James M. Hoppin]], [[George Edward Day (language scholar)|George Edward Day]], [[George Park Fisher]], and [[Leonard Bacon]]. The first Bachelor of Divinity (B.D.) was conferred in 1867, and the department became a separate School of Divinity in 1869. The school remained across from Old Campus until 1929, when a new campus was constructed on the northern edge of the university campus, at the top of [[Prospect Hill, New Haven|Prospect Hill]]. [[File:Sterling Divinity Quadrangle.jpg|thumb|right|Sterling Divinity Quadrangle]] [[Berkeley Divinity School]] affiliated with Yale Divinity School in 1971, and in the same year the university replaced the B.D. with a [[Master of Divinity|Master of Divinity (M.Div.)]] program. While Berkeley retains its [[Episcopal Church in the United States of America|Episcopal Church]] connection, its students are admitted by and fully enrolled as members of Yale Divinity School. [[The Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale University]], a division of the Divinity School, maintains a large collection of primary source materials about [[Jonathan Edwards (theologian)|Jonathan Edwards]], a 1720 Yale alumnus. The Yale Institute of Sacred Music (ISM) is jointly-affiliated with the Divinity School and School of Music. It offers programs in choral conducting, organ performance, voice, and church music studies, and in liturgical studies and religion and the arts. In May 2016, [[Andover Newton Theological School]] president [[Martin Copenhaver]] announced that Andover Newton would begin a process of formal affiliation with the Divinity School over the next two years. In the 2016–17 academic year, a cohort of faculty relocated to New Haven teaching students and launching pilot initiatives focused on congregational ministry education, while Andover Newton continued to operate in Massachusetts over the next two years. In July 2017, a formal affiliation was signed, resulting in smaller Andover Newton functioning as a unit within Yale Divinity School, similar to its arrangement with Berkeley.{{Cite web|url=http://divinity.yale.edu/news/yds-and-andover-newton-sign-historic-agreement|title=YDS and Andover Newton sign historic agreement|date=July 20, 2017|website=Yale Divinity School}} In October 2020, YDS received a $1 million grant from the Lilly Endowment as part of the foundation's Thriving Congregations Initiative to fund a program entitled, "Reimagining Church: New Models for the 21st Century." Reimagining Church will involve 40 congregations in Connecticut as well as YDS students, faculty, and staff over a five-year period.{{Cite web|title=With Lilly grant, YDS launches initiative reimagining church for 21st century {{!}} Yale Divinity School|url=https://divinity.yale.edu/news/lilly-grant-yds-launches-initiative-reimagining-church-21st-century|access-date=2021-03-18|website=divinity.yale.edu}} In November 2020, the Yale Divinity School Women's Center revived the publication of ''The Voice Journal of Literary and Theological Ideas'', a feminist journal that initially ran from 1996 to 2002.{{Cite web|last1=Brown|first1=Julia|first2=Madison|last2=Hahamy|title=Divinity students revive feminist journal|url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2020/11/05/divinity-students-revive-feminist-journal/|access-date=2021-03-18|website=[[Yale Daily News]]|date=5 November 2020|language=en}} === Deans === When the Divinity school was first established in 1822, there were no deans, instead the presidents of Yale presided over Divinity School faculty meetings. This occurred during the preseidencies of both [[Jeremiah Day]] (1817–1846) and [[Theodore Dwight Woolsey]] (1846–1871).{{Cite web |title=Deans of the Divinity School |url=https://divinity-adhoc.library.yale.edu/Exhibits/YDS_Deans_exhibit.pdf}} Beginning with the appointment of George Edward Day in 1888, there has been a dean of the Yale Divinity School. [[Gregory Sterling]], a [[New Testament]] scholar and [[Churches of Christ|Church of Christ]] pastor, has been the dean of the divinity school since 2012, succeeding New Testament scholar [[Harold W. Attridge]], who returned to teaching as a [[Sterling Professor]] upon completing two five-year terms as dean.{{Cite web|url=https://divinity.yale.edu/news/yds-dean-greg-sterling-reappointed-second-five-year-term|title=YDS Dean Greg Sterling reappointed to second five-year term {{!}} Yale Divinity School|website=divinity.yale.edu|access-date=2019-05-06}} The leaders of the affiliated seminaries are [[Andrew McGowan]], Dean and President of [[Berkeley Divinity School at Yale|Berkeley Divinity School]], and Sarah Drummond, Founding Dean of [[Andover Newton Seminary at Yale Divinity School|Andover Newton Seminary]] at Yale Divinity School. ==Campus== [[File:Yale Divinity School Highsmith.jpg|thumb|Sterling Divinity Quadrangle, campus of the Yale Divinity School]] When the department was organized as a school in 1869, it was moved to a campus across from the northwest corner of the [[New Haven Green]] composed of East Divinity Hall (1869), Marquand Chapel (1871), West Divinity Hall (1871), and the Trowbridge Library (1881). The buildings, designed by [[Richard Morris Hunt]], were demolished under the [[residential colleges of Yale University|residential college plan]] and replaced by [[Calhoun College|Calhoun College, now known as Grace Hopper College]].{{Cite web |url=http://www.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/01_03/popup/landmarks/12.html |title=Yale's Lost Landmarks: Divinity Hall, Yale Alumni Magazine |access-date=2007-11-06 |archive-date=2007-10-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071005200617/http://www.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/01_03/popup/landmarks/12.html |url-status=dead }} In 1929, the trustees of the estate of lawyer [[John William Sterling]] agreed that a portion of his bequest to Yale would be used to build a new campus for the Divinity School.{{cite book |last=Bedford |first=Steven |title=John Russell Popoe: Architect of Empire |publisher=Random House |location=New York |year=1998 |isbn=9780847820863 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/johnrussellpopea00bedf/page/166 166–168] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/johnrussellpopea00bedf/page/166 }} The Sterling Divinity Quadrangle, completed in 1932, is a [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]]-style complex built at the top of [[Prospect Hill (New Haven)|Prospect Hill]]. It was designed by [[Delano & Aldrich]] and modeled in part on the [[University of Virginia]]. [[File:YDS Courtyard.jpg|thumb|right|Courtyard at Sterling Divinity Quadrangle]] A $49-million renovation of Sterling Divinity Quadrangle was completed in 2003. The '''Humanities Quadrangle''' ('''HQ'''), originally the '''Hall of Graduate Studies''' ('''HGS'''), is an academic [[Quadrangle (architecture)|quadrangle]] at [[Yale University]] in [[New Haven, Connecticut]]. First opened in 1932, the building was designed as a [[Collegiate Gothic]] structure by architect [[James Gamble Rogers]]. After serving for 86 years as the home of faculty offices and graduate student housing for the [[Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences]], the Hall of Graduate Studies underwent a series of major renovations designed by [http://www.annumarchitects.com Annum Architects] (formerly Ann Beha Architects)<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gonzalez |first=Susan |date=2021-04-01 |title=Humanities Quadrangle: A cherished Yale icon reimagined |url=https://news.yale.edu/2021/04/01/humanities-quadrangle-cherished-yale-icon-reimagined |access-date=2024-09-12 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref> starting in 2018.

It reopened as the Humanities Quadrangle in 2021, now serving as the home of 15 academic departments and several humanities programs. With 311 offices, 28 classrooms, and 24 meeting spaces, the Humanities Quadrangle is frequently used by students and faculty.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Gonzalez |first=Susan |date=2021-04-01 |title=Humanities Quadrangle: A cherished Yale icon reimagined |url=https://news.yale.edu/2021/04/01/humanities-quadrangle-cherished-yale-icon-reimagined |access-date=2023-06-06 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref>  Among others, HQ houses [[Yale College]]'s Directed Studies program and the Whitney Humanities Center.

== History ==

=== Before academic use ===
Located at 320 York Street in [[New Haven, Connecticut]],<ref name=":0" /> the site of the Humanities Quadrangle has undergone significant changes throughout its past. A map from 1824 shows the area as largely undeveloped, aside from a few small buildings along the curb of York Street.<ref>{{cite map|author=Amos Doolittle|title=Plan of New Haven|date=1824-05-28|url=https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/15675074|scale=[ca. 1:3,750]|language=en|access-date=2023-06-06}}</ref> By 1852, part of the land belonged to the local [[Christ Church (New Haven)|Christ Church]],<ref>{{cite map|author=R. Whiteford|title=Map of the city of New Haven|year=1852|url=https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/15675092|scale=[ca. 1:15,840]|publisher=L.S. Punderson|language=en|access-date=2023-06-06}}</ref> and ownership was transferred to the [[New Haven Wheel Company]] by 1886.<ref>{{cite map|author=Sanborn Map & Publishing Co.|title=Insurance maps of New Haven, Connecticut. Volume 2.|year=1886|url=https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/11175977|scale=1:600|page=30|language=en|access-date=2023-06-06}}</ref> The company vacated its premises by 1901,<ref>{{cite map|author=Sanborn-Perris Map Co.|title=Insurance maps of New Haven, Connecticut. Volume 1.|year=1901|url=https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/11188890|scale=1:600|page=48|language=en|access-date=2023-06-06}}</ref> and buildings adjacent to the former wheel factory became [[North American fraternity and sorority housing|fraternity housing]] by 1924.<ref>{{cite map|author=Sanborn Map Company|title=Insurance maps of New Haven, Connecticut. Volume 2.|year=1924|url=https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/11190119|scale=1:600|page=206|language=en|access-date=2023-06-06}}</ref>

=== Original construction ===
In a February 1929 speech to recent graduates, [[Yale University]] President [[James Rowland Angell|James Angell]] announced plans for building a new [[Quadrangle (architecture)|quadrangle]] to house the [[Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences|Yale Graduate School]],<ref>{{Cite news |title=$4,000,000 ASSURED FOR YALE BUILDINGS; President Angell Tells Alumni Sterling Estate Will Provide $2,000,000 for Dormitories. LIKE SUM FOR GYMNASIUM Unnamed Source Promises These Funds--New Structure Will Be on Another Site. HOUSING PLANS EXTENSIVE Program Akin to Oxford and Cambridge Method--Faculty SalaryIncreases Recited to Graduates. Graduates Visit Classrooms. Gymnasium a "Winter Playground." Tells of Better Faculty Salaries. |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//arch-timesmachine-fe-prd-40741-2-575473780.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/timesmachine/1929/02/23/95737250.html?pageNumber=12 |access-date=2023-06-18}}</ref> and construction began the next year.<ref name=":022">{{Cite web |title=History of Yale Graduate School {{!}} Yale Graduate School of Arts & Sciences |url=https://gsas.yale.edu/deans-office/history-yale-graduate-school |access-date=2023-06-18 |website=gsas.yale.edu |archive-date=2021-08-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817115425/https://gsas.yale.edu/deans-office/history-yale-graduate-school |url-status=dead }}</ref> Some had expected this development to cause the demolition of [[Mory's]], but blueprints were drawn to exclude the historic restaurant.<ref>{{Cite news |title=FOR YALE GRADUATE SCHOOL; Plans Drawn Do Not Include Mory's Association Building. |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//timesmachine.content-tagging.us-east-1-01.prd.dvsp.nyt.net/timesmachine/1930/04/16/96098028.html?pageNumber=4 |access-date=2023-06-18}}</ref> Although $3.5 million was initially budgeted, the final cost was only $2.5 million, which was financed by funds from the estate of [[John William Sterling|John Sterling]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=YALE BUILDING OUTLAY PUT AT $28,000,000; Value of Structures Under Way Totals $20,000,000--Some to Be Ready This Fall. |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//arch-timesmachine-fe-prd-40741-2-575473780.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/timesmachine/1930/08/24/118186375.html?pageNumber=49 |access-date=2023-06-18}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite news |title=YALE BUILDINGS READY.; Seven Structures Are Completed for Opening of New Term. |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//arch-timesmachine-fe-prd-40741-2-575473780.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/timesmachine/1932/08/29/100846128.html?pageNumber=13 |access-date=2023-06-19}}</ref> The building was officially named after its benefactor,<ref name=":12" /> but the Sterling surname was dropped over time, leading to the Hall of Graduate Studies.<ref name=":022" />

The Hall of Graduate Studies opened its doors for the first time on September 29, 1932, coinciding with the start of the academic year. The new quadrangle included 80 offices, 16 classrooms, a 200-foot tower, and [[Dormitory|dormitories]] for 225 students.<ref>{{Cite news |title=YALE OPENS THURSDAY; NEW BUILDINGS READY; Gymnasium, Divinity Quadrangle and a Sheffield Addition Finished -- Faculty Changes Made. |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//arch-timesmachine-fe-prd-40741-2-575473780.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/timesmachine/1932/09/26/100854881.html?pageNumber=12 |access-date=2023-06-20}}</ref>

=== Modern renovations ===
[[File:Swensen Tower, Yale Humanities Quadrangle.jpg|thumb|right|upright=.65|[[David F. Swensen|Swensen]] Tower]]
In March 2015, Yale received a $25 million donation towards transforming the Hall of Graduate Studies into a center for the [[humanities]], which prompted the building's iconic 14-story tower to be named after [[David F. Swensen|David Swensen]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-03-25 |title=Gift to transform Hall of Graduate Studies honors David Swensen |url=https://news.yale.edu/2015/03/25/gift-transform-hall-graduate-studies-honors-david-swensen |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref> In addition, another $50 million was provided by an anonymous donor in January 2016,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-19 |title=$50 million gift to help fund humanities hub, create endowment |url=https://news.yale.edu/2016/01/19/50-million-gift-help-fund-humanities-hub-create-endowment |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref> contributing to a total budget of $162 million.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Connolly |first=Bess |date=2019-08-19 |title=New Yale humanities hub honored for its excellence in planning |url=https://news.yale.edu/2019/08/19/new-yale-humanities-hub-honored-its-excellence-planning |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref> By September 2017, the city's [[Board of Alderman|Board of Alders]] approved the new site plans,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-09-19 |title=Grad Housing Conversion Gets Alder OK |url=https://www.newhavenindependent.org/article/hgs_conversion_ |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=New Haven Independent |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite report |url=https://www.newhavenct.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/13610/637883172708970000 |title=New Haven City Plan Commission Site Plan Review |last=Mattison |first=Edward |date=2017-09-19 |access-date=2023-07-02}}</ref> and construction began in August 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Feibel |first=Adelaide |date=2018-08-30 |title=Construction begins on HGS renovations |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2018/08/30/construction-begins-on-hgs-renovations/ |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=Yale Daily News |language=en}}</ref>

The renovations were originally slated to be done by 2020, but delays due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] caused the project to finish a year behind schedule. The building officially reopened on February 15, 2021 as the Humanities Quadrangle, although some facilities were not completed until May 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hahamy |first=Madison |date=2021-03-11 |title=Humanities Quadrangle opens its doors — to some |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2021/03/11/humanities-quadrangle-opens-its-doors-to-some/ |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=Yale Daily News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Decker |first=Maia |date=2021-05-04 |title=Humanities Quadrangle serves as new home to 15 departments |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2021/05/04/humanities-quadrangle-serves-as-new-home-to-15-departments/ |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=Yale Daily News |language=en}}</ref> About 13,000 square feet of underground space was added during renovations, resulting in a total floor area of 173,811 square feet.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Architecture ==

=== Finnegan's contributions ===
During construction of the Hall of Graduate Studies, a man known only as Mr. Finnegan was placed in charge of building operations. Finnegan was tasked with executing [[James Gamble Rogers]]'s plans, but he made modifications to express a personal disdain for the self-importance of graduate schools.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Furniss |first=Edgar Stevenson |title=The Graduate School of Yale: A Brief History |publisher=Carl Purington Rollins Printing-Office |year=1965 |pages=69–72 |language=en |asin=B0007DU7RG}}</ref>
[[File:Yale Humanities Quadrangle Angel Brick.jpg|thumb|One of Finnegan's special bricks in the Yale Humanities Quadrangle, with an angel carving.]]
The first of the unauthorized changes was the use of bricks with unique carvings. Although [[Yale University|Yale]] had requested bricks with its name emblazoned on the surface, Finnegan created additional designs to represent senior university officials. These included an angel ([[James Rowland Angell|James Angell]]), a Maltese cross ([[Wilbur Lucius Cross|Wilbur Cross]]), and a furnace ([[Edgar S. Furniss|Edgar Furniss]]).<ref name=":2" /> Many of the special bricks can still be seen in the building's lobby.

Finnegan also directed the installation of lifelike busts of Rogers and Thomas Farnam, the university's [[comptroller]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=THOMAS W. FARNAM; Former Yale Official, a Leader of Red Cross in World War |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//arch-timesmachine-fe-prd-40741-2-575473780.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/timesmachine/1943/08/04/83933644.html?pageNumber=17 |access-date=2023-07-03}}</ref> The busts were displayed prominently within the building's [[portico]], and they were discovered by Farnam himself during an inspection visit. Farnam demanded for the sculptures to be removed, but workers were only able to whittle them down into the resemblance of Egyptian [[pharaoh]]s.<ref name=":2" />

After the Hall of Graduate Studies opened, a previously unnoticed inscription was found on the archway of the building's entrance. The text was from the novel [[Scaramouche (novel)|Scaramouche]] by [[Rafael Sabatini]], stating that "He was born with a gift for laughter and a sense that the world was mad." University officials were upset by the inscription's non-scholarly origin, and after a brief investigation, it was revealed that Finnegan was responsible for the unsanctioned chiseling. However, Rogers would go on to claim that the text was proposed by a committee of Yale faculty.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite news |title=HERETICAL CARVING AT YALE IS TRACED; Faculty Itself Chose Excerpt From Best-Seller to Grace Portal, Architect Says. NEVER LOOKED AT, ANYWAY Inscriptions Chosen Chiefly if They Fit in Space and Cast Good Shadows, He Explains. |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.comhttp//arch-timesmachine-fe-prd-40741-2-575473780.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/timesmachine/1934/11/17/95496363.html?pageNumber=17 |access-date=2023-07-03}}</ref>

=== Entryway stone heads ===
The archway above the entrance of the building also features 12 stone heads, which face incoming foot traffic from the street. They represent a selection of the 85 [[Drafter|draftsmen]] who worked on the construction of the Hall of Graduate Studies, but only 11 surnames have been associated with the carvings. Unlike the adjacent textual inscription by Finnegan, the stone heads were approved in advance by the site's architects.<ref>{{Cite web |title=THE STONE HEADS OF 320 YORK {{!}} Whitney Humanities Center |url=https://whc.yale.edu/stone-heads-320-york |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=whc.yale.edu}}</ref>

== Other ==
In May 2018, the building was the site of an incident where a Black Yale graduate student was reported to the police for napping in her dorm's common room. The early morning encounter was streamed on [[Facebook live|Facebook Live]] and sparked controversy over [[racial profiling]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Griggs |first=Brandon |date=2018-05-09 |title=A black Yale graduate student took a nap in her dorm's common room. So a white student called police |url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/05/09/us/yale-student-napping-black-trnd/index.html |access-date=2023-06-06 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref>
